name: Micronesian
line: Hold your course in your head, use little, set something aside to recover and make things good for each other.

quote.text: We sweat and cry salt water, so we know that the ocean is really in our blood.
quote.source: A poet and scholar of Banaban and I-Kiribati descent. Quoted by Epeli Hau’ofa at the head of The Ocean in Us, 1997

quotes.text: I vow to tread lightly, act kindly and explore mindfully.
quotes.source: Stamped in the passport of every visitor to Palau since 2017 and signed on arrival. It is addressed to the children of Palau

quotes.text: Kindness is life, cruelty is death.
quotes.source: Jouj eo mour eo, lāj eo mej eo. A common English rendering

quotes.by: National motto of the Marshall Islands

quotes.text: We deserve to do more than just survive. We deserve to thrive.
quotes.source: From her poem Dear Matafele Peinam, spoken to her baby daughter before the United Nations Climate Summit, 23 September 2014

quotes.text: To navigate you must be brave, and to be brave you must remember.
quotes.source: The master navigator of Satawal, as his teaching is often summed up by his students

words.usage: A way of tracking a voyage. The navigator pictures the canoe as still and an unseen island off to one side as sliding backward beneath the stars, stage by stage.
One who has been initiated into the knowledge of the stars and the sea, and who is responsible for the lives of the crew.
A ceremony of several days in which masters pass on their knowledge and their authority. Mau Piailug held one in 2007, the first on Satawal in more than fifty years.
A single hull with an outrigger always kept to windward, and a sail that is carried from one end to the other to change direction. Among the fastest craft of the pre-industrial world.

words.meaning: A chart of sticks and shells
words.usage: A frame of palm ribs lashed together to show how ocean swells bend and cross around whole chains of atolls. Studied on land and never taken to sea.

words.meaning: Making things good for each other
words.usage: The central value of the people of the Marianas. Harmony kept by mutual help, with the good of the family ahead of the individual.

words.meaning: A gift that keeps a tie alive
words.usage: Help in money, food or labour given at weddings, christenings and funerals, remembered by both families and returned at the next occasion.
Shown above all to elders and to the ancestral spirits of the land, whose leave is asked before entering the jungle.

words.meaning: Greeting an elder by taking the scent of the hand
words.usage: A younger person lifts the back of an elder’s hand to the nose and is answered with a blessing.
The greeting of Guam and the Northern Marianas. Thank you is si Yu’os ma’åse’.

words.meaning: A stone pillar with a cup-shaped capstone
words.usage: Set in two rows to carry the houses of the ancient CHamoru. They are now the emblem of the Marianas.
Greeting, farewell and affection in one word. It is often explained as you are a rainbow.
The group that holds land. In the Marshalls, as in most of Micronesia, land rights pass through women.
The head of the senior lineage, who holds the land in trust with the workers and the heads of families.
Woven by women from pandanus leaf with intricate borders, once worn as clothing. The art has been revived since 2006.
The greeting of Kiribati. Thank you is ko rabwa.
A vast thatched roof on low coral posts, at the centre of every village in Kiribati. Each family has its inherited sitting place beneath it.

words.meaning: A request that should not be refused
words.usage: Asking a relative or friend for something of theirs. To refuse is shameful, and the giver may ask in turn.
Said on meeting and parting. Thank you is kalahngan.
The root is pounded on a great flat stone that rings like a bell, and squeezed through hibiscus bark. The first cups go to the chiefs in order.
The head of one of the five kingdoms of Pohnpei, addressed in a special language of honour.
The principle of Pohnpeian life. It is shown in speech, posture and the order of service at feasts.
Discs of pale stone with a hole in the middle, up to three and a half metres across, quarried in Palau and brought four hundred kilometres by canoe. Their worth lies in their history.
A tall thatched house by the shore where young men lived, learned fishing and navigation and looked out for canoes.
The everyday greeting. Thank you is sulang.
A high-gabled house raised on stone, its beams and front painted with rows of pictures that tell the village’s stories.

words.meaning: A ban declared by the chiefs
words.usage: A stretch of reef or a species is closed to all taking for a time, so that it can recover. The basis of Palau’s modern marine reserves.
The greeting of the islands of Chuuk. Thank you is kinisou.
The greeting of Yap. Thank you is kammagar.
Sharing, respect and care for family. A national day is given to it each September.

practices.name: Declare a bul
practices.instructions: Choose one thing that you have been taking too much of: a food, a screen, a shop, a habit, a person’s patience, a stretch of ground. This morning, declare it closed. Say aloud what is closed and for how long, a day, a week or the month, and tell someone so that it is public. Then keep the ban strictly until it ends. When it is over, return to the thing with care and notice what has recovered.
practices.why: In Palau, when the chiefs saw that a reef was being fished out, they placed a bul on it, and no one took anything from that place until it was lifted. The custom is very old and is still law. In 2015 Palau used the same principle to close four-fifths of its ocean waters to all fishing.
variations: Set aside one day a week on which you buy nothing.
Close a part of your garden, and leave it wild.
Read the Palau Pledge and write one for your own home.

practices.name: Use water as on an atoll
practices.instructions: Live today as if your fresh water came from a rain tank that will not be refilled this week. Wash in a basin, not under a running tap. Turn the tap off between uses. Catch what you can and use it twice. Throw no food away. At the end of the day, reckon roughly how much water you used, and where the rest of what you usually use goes.
practices.why: A coral atoll is a ring of sand a few metres high with no rivers and no lakes. Its people live on rain caught from roofs and a thin lens of fresh water that floats on the salt beneath the sand. In a drought every cup is counted. Micronesians built complete and lasting societies on some of the scarcest land and water on Earth.
variations: Find out where your tap water comes from and how much of it there is.

practices.name: Find your way without a device
practices.instructions: Make one journey today on foot with your phone put away. Before you set out, fix the route in your mind and choose a landmark off to one side. As you go, keep track of where you are by how that landmark shifts against what is behind it. Notice the direction of the sun and the wind. At the end, turn and point straight back to where you started.
practices.why: The navigators of the Caroline Islands sail for days out of sight of land with no instruments and no chart. They hold the whole voyage in the mind, steering by a memorised compass of rising and setting stars and marking progress by an unseen reference island that seems to move backward along the horizon. The system is called etak. The navigator sleeps very little.
variations: Learn the points where the sun rises and sets from your home, and how they move through the year.
Draw a map of your neighbourhood from memory.
Walk home by a way you have never taken.

practices.name: Make it good for each other
practices.instructions: Find out what is happening in your wider family and circle this week: a birth, a wedding, a move, an illness, a death, an exam. Choose one and contribute something real, in food, money, work or time, without waiting to be asked. Let them know they can count on you. Remember, without writing it down, what others have given you at such times, and see that it is returned.
practices.why: CHamoru families are bound by chenchule’, the giving of help at every important family event, which is remembered and answered at the next. Behind it stands inafa’maolek, the principle that each person is responsible for making things good for the others. Across Micronesia a request from kin is not refused, and the catch is shared before anyone eats.
variations: Cook for a family that has a new baby or a death.
Give your labour at someone’s celebration.
Divide something good that came to you today among your household.

practices.name: Plait, weave or lash
practices.instructions: Spend twenty minutes making something with cord or fibre and your hands. Plait three strands into a rope. Learn one knot or one lashing and tie it ten times until your fingers know it. Weave a small mat from strips of paper or leaf. Work slowly and evenly, undo what is uneven and do it again. Sit with others while you work if you can, and talk.
practices.why: On islands without metal, everything was held together by cord. Canoe planks were sewn with twine of coconut husk fibre rolled on the thigh, a single voyaging canoe needing kilometres of it, and houses were lashed in patterns that were both strong and beautiful. Women plaited sails, baskets and fine mats from pandanus leaf.
variations: Learn the bowline and the clove hitch.
Mend something with a proper whipping or lashing.
Plait a strip of leaves into a band.

tasks.name: Listen to the choirs of Kiribati
tasks.meta: Listen · massed voices and clapped rhythm

tasks.name: Look at a Marshallese stick chart
tasks.meta: Art · a map of how the sea moves

tasks.name: Play chonka
tasks.meta: Games · the sowing game of the Marianas

tasks.name: Journal: what do you hold in your head that you used to keep on a device?
What is a thing worth when everyone knows its story?
Greet the oldest person you meet with special respect
Go without one thing today so that it lasts
Step outside after dark and find one star you can name
Weave or plait three strands of anything
Watch the waves, or the wind in trees, and read the direction
Share a coconut, or anything sweet, with a neighbour

rules.why: Know where you are and where you are going without being told.
Water, food and land are short. Take what you need and waste nothing.
Close what is overused until it has recovered.

rules.text: Make it good for each other
rules.why: Give at every family need, and remember what was given to you.
They hold the knowledge and the land. Greet them first.
What comes from the sea belongs to the village before it belongs to you.

read.title: The Last Navigator
read.creator: Stephen D. Thomas
read.why: A young American spends two seasons on Satawal learning from Mau Piailug, who feared that his knowledge would die with him.

read.title: Iep Jāltok: Poems from a Marshallese Daughter
read.creator: Kathy Jetñil-Kijiner
read.why: Poems on nuclear testing, migration, racism and rising seas. The title is a basket whose opening faces the speaker, a name for a girl child.

read.title: Sweat and Salt Water: Selected Works
read.creator: Teresia Kieuea Teaiwa
read.why: Essays and poems by a founder of Pacific studies, on militarism, tourism, feminism and the ocean.

read.title: from unincorporated territory [åmot]
read.creator: Craig Santos Perez
read.why: The fifth book of a long poem about Guam by a CHamoru poet. Åmot means medicine.

read.title: East Is a Big Bird: Navigation and Logic on Puluwat Atoll
read.creator: Thomas Gladwin
read.why: A careful account of how Carolinian navigators think, written to show that it is a rigorous science.

read.title: Consuming Ocean Island
read.creator: Katerina Martina Teaiwa
read.why: How Banaba was mined away for phosphate to fertilise the farms of Australia and New Zealand, and what became of its people.

watch.title: Papa Mau: The Wayfinder
watch.creator: Nā’ālehu Anthony
watch.why: The life of Mau Piailug and his decision to teach navigation to people outside his own island.

watch.title: The Navigators: Pathfinders of the Pacific
watch.creator: Sanford Low
watch.why: Mau on Satawal, with the archaeology of the settlement of the Pacific.

watch.title: Radio Bikini
watch.creator: Robert Stone
watch.why: The 1946 atomic tests at Bikini told through the military’s own film, a sailor who was there and the chief of the people who were moved.

watch.title: Anote’s Ark
watch.creator: Matthieu Rytz
watch.why: The president of Kiribati travels the world asking what will happen to a nation whose land is two metres high.

listen.title: Spirit of Micronesia
listen.creator: Field recordings by David Fanshawe
listen.why: Chants, dance songs and hymns recorded across the islands in the 1970s and 1980s.

listen.title: Kiribati choral dance songs
listen.creator: Village choirs of Kiribati
listen.why: Dozens of voices in close harmony with clapping and a beaten box, rising to a shout.

listen.title: Kantan Chamorrita
listen.creator: CHamoru singers
listen.why: Improvised verses sung back and forth between two people or groups to an old tune, teasing and answering each other.

listen.title: Marshallese roro
listen.creator: Chanters of the Marshall Islands
listen.why: Short rhythmic chants used to give strength for hauling canoes, for navigation and for telling history.

art.title: Stick charts
art.creator: Marshallese navigators
art.why: Lattices of palm ribs with shells for islands, showing the swells a canoe will feel as it nears land. Each was made and understood by one navigator.

art.title: Storyboards
art.creator: Palauan carvers
art.why: Legends carved in relief on planks, a form that grew from the painted beams of the meeting house.

art.title: Jaki-ed
art.creator: Marshallese weavers
art.why: Square clothing mats with borders of fine geometric patterning in brown, black and white.

art.title: Coconut fibre armour
art.creator: The warriors of Kiribati
art.why: Full suits of knotted coconut cord with a high back plate, worn with a helmet made from the skin of a porcupine fish.

eat.title: Breadfruit
eat.creator: Roasted, boiled, or preserved in pits
eat.why: The main food of the high islands. Fermented breadfruit paste keeps for years and saw people through storms and droughts.

eat.title: Kelaguen and red rice
eat.creator: Chopped chicken or fish with lemon, coconut and hot pepper
eat.why: The dish of every CHamoru party table, beside rice coloured with achote seeds.

eat.title: Giant swamp taro
eat.creator: Babai, grown in pits dug down to the water
eat.why: The prestige food of Kiribati. A plant may be tended for years before it is given at a feast.

eat.title: Pandanus paste
eat.creator: Mokwan, a dried fruit leather
eat.why: Marshallese voyaging food. Cooked pandanus pulp is dried and rolled tight in leaves.

drink.title: Sakau
drink.creator: Fresh kava of Pohnpei
drink.why: Thick and strong. It is drunk slowly at dusk from a coconut shell, and conversation falls quiet.

drink.title: Coconut toddy
drink.creator: Sap tapped from the flower stalk
drink.why: Collected morning and evening by a cutter who sings in the treetop. Sweet when fresh, and rich in vitamins.

drink.title: Drinking coconut
drink.creator: A green nut
drink.why: The safest water on an atoll.

customs.title: The first birthday
customs.creator: Kemem
customs.why: Marshallese families hold their largest feast when a child reaches one year, in thanks for a life once far from certain.

customs.title: The place in the meeting house
customs.creator: Sitting where your family sits
customs.why: In a Kiribati maneaba each clan has its own spot under the roof. A visitor is shown where to sit and speaks only when invited.

customs.title: Stone money stays where it is
customs.creator: Ownership by memory
customs.why: A large rai is not moved when it changes hands. Everyone simply knows whose it now is.

customs.title: Asking leave of the ancestors
customs.creator: A word before entering
customs.why: On Guam one asks permission of the spirits of the old people before going into the jungle or taking from it.

games.title: Model canoe racing
games.creator: Riwut · Marshall Islands
games.why: Boys and men build small outrigger canoes with leaf sails and race them across the lagoon, wading after them.

games.title: The Micronesian all-around
games.creator: Athletics · Micronesian Games
games.why: Five events in one contest: climbing a coconut palm, husking nuts, grating coconut, throwing a spear and swimming and diving.

games.title: Chonka
games.creator: Board game · Mariana Islands
games.why: A sowing game played with shells in two rows of seven pits.

games.title: Oreano
games.creator: Ball game · Kiribati
games.why: Two teams throw a heavy stone ball wrapped in coconut fibre, and a side scores when the other fails to catch it.

festivals.title: Yap Day
festivals.creator: 1 and 2 March, Yap
festivals.why: Villages compete in sitting, standing and bamboo stick dances, with canoe sailing and traditional skills.

festivals.title: Manit Day
festivals.creator: The last Friday of September, Marshall Islands
festivals.why: A day of Marshallese custom: weaving, husking, canoe racing, food and song.

festivals.title: Kiribati Independence Day
festivals.creator: 12 July
festivals.why: A week of choir and dance competitions, canoe races and sport in the capital.

festivals.title: Nuclear Victims Remembrance Day
festivals.creator: 1 March, Marshall Islands
festivals.why: The anniversary of the Bravo test of 1954. A day of mourning and of testimony by survivors.

places.title: Nan Madol
places.creator: Pohnpei, Federated States of Micronesia
places.why: Nearly a hundred artificial islets built on a reef from stacked basalt columns between about 1200 and 1600, the seat of a dynasty of rulers. A World Heritage site.

places.title: The Rock Islands
places.creator: Palau
places.why: Hundreds of green limestone islands in a turquoise lagoon, with marine lakes and the remains of old stone villages. A World Heritage site.

places.title: The House of Taga
places.creator: Tinian, Northern Mariana Islands
places.why: The tallest latte stones ever raised, five metres high. One of the original twelve still stands.

places.title: The stone money banks
places.creator: Yap, Federated States of Micronesia
places.why: Rows of rai leaning along village paths, each with an owner and a history known to all.

places.title: Bikini Atoll
places.creator: Marshall Islands
places.why: The site of twenty-three nuclear tests. Its people were moved in 1946 and have not been able to return. A World Heritage site.

places.title: Leluh
places.creator: Kosrae, Federated States of Micronesia
places.why: The walled compounds, canals and royal tombs of a city of basalt and coral that flourished about 1400.

ethics.title: Respect
ethics.text: For elders, chiefs, ancestors and the land.
ethics.practice: Greet an older person first today and ask how they are.

ethics.title: Sharing
ethics.text: No one eats while a neighbour goes without.
ethics.practice: Divide something before you take your part.

ethics.title: Restraint
ethics.text: Take only what the island can replace.
ethics.practice: Leave the last of something for someone else.

ethics.title: Mutual help
ethics.text: Be there at every family occasion.
ethics.practice: Offer help to a relative before they ask.

ethics.title: Humility
ethics.text: Do not set yourself above others or speak loudly of yourself.

ethics.title: Courage
ethics.text: The sea is not safe, and the navigator goes anyway.
ethics.practice: Do the thing you are putting off out of fear.

philosophy.title: The canoe stands still
philosophy.text: In etak the navigator thinks of the canoe as fixed and the islands as moving past. A change of viewpoint makes the problem solvable.
philosophy.practice: What would change if you treated yourself as the still point?

philosophy.title: Knowledge held in the person
philosophy.text: The navigator carries the star compass, the swells and the sea marks in memory. Nothing is written down.
philosophy.practice: What do you truly know without looking it up?

philosophy.title: Value as shared memory
philosophy.text: A stone that lies at the bottom of the sea can still be owned and spent, because everyone knows its story.
philosophy.practice: What makes your own money worth anything?

philosophy.title: Land through the mother
philosophy.text: In most of Micronesia land and rank pass through women.
philosophy.practice: What did you inherit through your mother’s line?

philosophy.title: Small land, great ocean
philosophy.text: The islands are tiny and the sea between them is vast, and people thought of the sea as their own.
philosophy.practice: What do you call small that is really large?

philosophy.title: Enough
philosophy.text: Scarcity taught careful use and constant sharing.
philosophy.practice: How much is enough for you?

philosophy.title: The closing
philosophy.text: A thing protected for a time comes back stronger.
philosophy.practice: What in your life needs to be left alone?

philosophy.title: The first to go under
philosophy.text: People who did least to warm the world may lose their whole country to the sea.
philosophy.practice: What do you owe to those who pay for your comfort?

intro: Micronesia, the small islands, is the name given to some two thousand islands scattered across the western Pacific, most of them north of the equator. Their total land area is smaller than Luxembourg, spread over an ocean larger than the United States. They include the high volcanic islands of the Marianas, Palau, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae and the low coral atolls of the outer Carolines, the Marshall Islands and Kiribati. Today the region is divided among the Federated States of Micronesia, Palau, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati and Nauru, with Guam and the Northern Marianas under the United States.

The name suggests one people, and there are many. The islands were settled from at least two directions. The Marianas were reached about 1500 BC, probably from the Philippines, in a crossing of some two thousand kilometres that was the longest sea voyage anyone had yet made. Palau was settled soon after. The eastern islands were reached about two thousand years ago by people coming north from Melanesia. More than twenty languages are spoken, and a CHamoru from Guam and an I-Kiribati have as little in common in speech and custom as a Spaniard and a Finn.

What they share was shaped by the sea and by smallness. An atoll is a ring of sand a few metres high, with no rivers, thin soil and only the rain to drink. Its people lived on breadfruit, coconut, taro grown in pits, and fish, and survived storms and droughts through networks of exchange with other islands. They became some of the finest sailors in history. Carolinian navigators crossed hundreds of kilometres of open sea by the stars, tracking their progress with the system called etak. Marshallese navigators learned to feel how swells bend around distant atolls and recorded the patterns in charts of sticks.

In most of the islands, land and rank pass through the mother’s line, and chiefs hold the land in trust for their lineage. On the high islands, powerful societies raised monuments in stone: the latte pillars of the Marianas, the stone money of Yap, quarried in Palau and carried home by canoe, and Nan Madol on Pohnpei, a ceremonial city of basalt columns built on a reef.

Outsiders came early and stayed long. Magellan landed on Guam in 1521, and Spain conquered the Marianas in the late seventeenth century at the cost of most of the CHamoru population. The other islands passed from Spain to Germany, then in 1914 to Japan, and in 1945 to the United States, after some of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific war. Between 1946 and 1958 the United States exploded sixty-seven nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak in the Marshall Islands. The people of several atolls were moved or exposed to fallout, and some have never gone home. Banaba and Nauru were stripped for phosphate.

Most of the islands became self-governing between 1968 and 1994. They now face a new threat. The atoll nations stand barely two metres above a rising sea, and their leaders and poets have become some of the clearest voices on climate change. At home the old skills are being taught again, in canoe houses and weaving circles.
This Onda takes its practices from the disciplines of small-island life: the closing, the careful use of water, finding the way, mutual help and work with cord.
guide.origin: The islands of the western Pacific north of the equator: the Marianas, Palau, the Carolines, the Marshalls, Kiribati and Nauru
guide.era: The Mariana Islands were settled about 1500 BC. Around half a million Micronesians live in the islands today

figures.name: Isokelekel
figures.bio: A warrior who, in Pohnpeian tradition, came from Kosrae with 333 companions, overthrew the tyrant rulers of Nan Madol and founded the present system of chiefs.

figures.name: Hurao
figures.bio: A CHamoru chief of Guam who rallied some two thousand warriors against the Spanish. A speech attributed to him by a French Jesuit is the first recorded CHamoru protest against colonial rule.

figures.name: Mau Piailug
figures.bio: A master navigator of Satawal, initiated as a boy. He guided Hōkūle’a to Tahiti in 1976 and, against custom, taught his art to Hawaiians so that it would not be lost.

figures.name: Tosiwo Nakayama
figures.bio: Born on a small atoll to a Japanese father and a Chuukese mother. He led the negotiations with the United States and was the first president of the Federated States of Micronesia.

figures.name: Amata Kabua
figures.bio: A high chief and the first president of the Marshall Islands. He wrote the words and music of its anthem.

figures.name: Darlene Keju
figures.bio: A Marshallese health worker who told the world in 1983 that many more islands had been contaminated than the United States admitted, and founded a youth health movement.

figures.name: Lijon Eknilang
figures.bio: She was seven on Rongelap when the ash of the Bravo test fell like snow. She testified about its effects on her people before the International Court of Justice.

figures.name: Tony deBrum
figures.bio: He watched the Bravo test as a boy of nine, helped win Marshallese independence and led the coalition of nations that secured the 1.5 degree goal in the Paris Agreement.

figures.name: Ieremia Tabai
figures.bio: The first president of Kiribati, elected at twenty-nine. He insisted that the country live within its own means.

figures.name: Anote Tong
figures.bio: President of Kiribati from 2003 to 2016, who bought land in Fiji and spoke of migration with dignity for his people.

figures.name: Teresia Teaiwa
figures.bio: Poet and teacher of Banaban, I-Kiribati and African American descent, raised in Fiji, who founded the first university programme in Pacific studies.

figures.name: Kathy Jetñil-Kijiner
figures.bio: Marshallese poet and climate envoy, whose poem to her daughter brought world leaders to their feet at the United Nations in 2014.

history.detail: Seafarers from island South-East Asia reach Guam and Saipan across two thousand kilometres of open ocean.
The western high islands are settled, and later the Marshalls, Kiribati, Pohnpei and Kosrae from the south.
CHamoru build houses on rows of stone pillars. Rice is grown, the only place in the Pacific where it was.
The rulers of Pohnpei and Kosrae build cities of basalt on the reef. Yap dominates the atolls to its east through a system of tribute and exchange.
The first Europeans to cross the Pacific land on Guam. After a dispute over a boat they burn a village.
A Jesuit mission is followed by thirty years of war. Disease and fighting reduce the CHamoru from perhaps fifty thousand to fewer than four thousand.
Germany takes the Marshall Islands and, after Spain’s defeat by the United States, buys the Carolines and the Northern Marianas. Guam goes to the United States.
Japan seizes the German islands and settles them heavily. By 1940 Japanese outnumber islanders.
Tarawa, Kwajalein, Saipan, Guam and Peleliu are fought over at great cost. The aircraft that bomb Hiroshima and Nagasaki take off from Tinian.
The United States explodes sixty-seven nuclear weapons in the Marshall Islands. The Bravo shot of 1 March 1954 is a thousand times the size of the Hiroshima bomb.
Nauru becomes independent in 1968 and Kiribati in 1979. The Marshall Islands and the Federated States enter free association with the United States in 1986, and Palau in 1994.
Mau Piailug guides Hōkūle’a from Hawai’i to Tahiti and begins the revival of voyaging across the Pacific.
Mau initiates sixteen navigators, five of them Hawaiian, in the first such ceremony on his island for half a century.
The Marshall Islands lead the push for a limit of 1.5 degrees of warming. Palau closes eighty per cent of its waters to fishing.

concepts.detail: A voyage is divided into stages by the bearing of an island off to one side as it passes under successive stars. The navigator keeps the count in his head for days.

concepts.text: The horizon as a ring of stars.
concepts.detail: Thirty-two points where known stars rise and set. It is taught to boys with pebbles laid in a circle on a mat.
Marshallese navigators lie in the hull and feel how the dominant swells are bent and reflected by atolls still far out of sight.
Clans and their land are traced through the mother. A man works his wife’s or his mother’s land, and children belong to her clan.
A rai is worth more if it was hard to bring home or if men died for it. Ownership passes by public agreement without moving the stone.
Atolls sent tribute of mats and cord to Yap each year and could call on help after a typhoon. Ties of clan linked islands hundreds of kilometres apart.
Chiefs barred the taking of fish, turtles or crops for a set time. Modern protected areas across Micronesia are built on this.

concepts.text: Small states and a great power.
concepts.detail: Three nations govern themselves while the United States holds military rights and their citizens may live and work there. A third of Marshallese now do.
Displacement, cancers and contaminated land remain from the tests. A concrete dome on Enewetak holds radioactive waste a few metres above the sea.

facts.text: Kiribati is pronounced Kiribas. The name is the local form of Gilberts.
Kiribati is the only country that lies in all four hemispheres, and its eastern islands are the first place on Earth to see each new day.
The largest stone money disc on Yap is about three and a half metres across and weighs some four tons.
The bikini swimsuit was named in 1946, four days after the first test at the atoll.
The highest natural point in the Marshall Islands is about ten metres above the sea.
CHamoru were the first Pacific Islanders to meet Europeans and were growing rice long before they did.

sensitivity.note: Micronesia is a label that outsiders gave to many distinct peoples. This Onda was written from published sources, names the language and island each word comes from, and should be reviewed by Micronesian readers.
requiredCaveats: Navigation is sacred knowledge in the Carolines, passed on through initiation. The practice here borrows only the idea of finding your way with attention, not the teaching itself.
Customs differ from island to island. What holds on Yap may be unknown on Guam or in Kiribati.
Nuclear testing, displacement and the rising sea are present realities for these communities, not history.
Spellings and pronunciations follow common English-language sources and are approximate.
